Section 01What this paper makes possible

A large polariton ensemble presents two different difficulties. There may be many quantum amplitudes to propagate, and there may be many bath trajectories to average. This paper attacks the first difficulty without replacing the molecular ensemble by a single effective molecule. It retains local molecular energies, local vibrational environments, and nonuniform light–matter couplings, but reorganizes the numerical operations so that zero matrix elements are never multiplied or stored.

The two central ingredients are a matrix-free action of the Holstein–Tavis–Cummings Hamiltonian and a Chebyshev expansion of the short-time quantum propagator. A third ingredient—separating excitation manifolds and their reference energies—prevents a large optical carrier frequency from setting the numerical cost of every quantum update. The paper combines these ingredients with Lindblad–partially linearized density matrix dynamics, abbreviated L-PLDM, to compute linear spectra.

These notes derive the model, the sparse operations, the polynomial propagator, the optical response, and the forward–backward trajectory representation. Every matrix is accompanied by its ordered basis. The appended Python program checks the algebra against independent dense constructions. Its absorption demo is a finite, bath-free disordered ensemble with a specified homogeneous broadening, not the article's full L-PLDM calculation.

The speedup is not a new physical approximation: sparse multiplication computes the same product as a dense matrix. A truncated Chebyshev expansion has a controllable numerical error. The molecular dynamics approximation remains a separate question, determined by the chosen trajectory method and bath treatment.

Primary source: published article, especially Secs. II–IV and Appendices A–C. These notes use the article's main text and its included appendices. Equation numbers below belong to this tutorial, not the paper.

Section 02Notation, units, and the different spaces

We use energies ϵn, Ec=ℏωc, and vn=ℏgn. Thus vn, not gn, appears in an energy-valued Hamiltonian matrix. An angular frequency and an energy are interchangeable only after explicitly setting ℏ=1. To convert a spectroscopic wavenumber ν~ into energy, use E=hcν~; the corresponding angular frequency is 2πcν~.

The quantum system consists of the molecular electronic states and one cavity photon mode. The environment consists of independent harmonic modes attached to each molecule:

HS=(⨂n=1NHn)⊗Hc,HB=⨂n=1N⨂α=1MnHnα.
(1)

An operator on one factor is implicitly embedded with identities on all other factors, but the first definitions below make that embedding explicit. The full density operator ρ^SB acts on HS⊗HB. Its reduced system density operator is ρ^S=TrBρ^SB. A trajectory's forward–backward dyad is an estimator of this operator; it need not itself be a normalized physical density operator.

A coefficient column |c⟩B is the coordinate representation of a state in the ordered basis B. A nuclear coordinate column |R⟩ contains classical numbers once a mixed quantum–classical approximation has been made. We reserve hats for operators and use bras and kets for vectors in either setting.

Section 03Local raising, lowering, and population matrices

For molecule n, choose the ordered local basis Bn=(|gn⟩,|en⟩). The molecular raising operator creates one excitation but cannot create a second excitation on the same molecule:

[σ^n]Bn=(0100),[σ^n†]Bn=(0010),[n^n]Bn=(0001).
(2)

Here n^n=σ^n†σ^n. Multiplication of these matrices gives

σ^n2=0,(σ^n†)2=0,[σ^n,σ^n†]=I^n−2n^n.
(3)

This is a two-level, or hard-core, excitation algebra. Operators on different molecules commute because they act on different tensor factors. The cavity has a different algebra: a^|q⟩=q|q−1⟩. In (|0⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩), its truncated matrix is

[a^]=(010002000),[a^†a^]=diag(0,1,2).
(4)

The 2 element is essential to the two-excitation Hamiltonian. A truncated oscillator does not satisfy the infinite-dimensional commutator at its upper boundary. This is harmless only when the retained excitation space is sufficient for the process being computed.

Section 04The full Hamiltonian and the bath energy convention

The model is

H^SB=H^S⊗I^B+I^S⊗H^B+∑nn^n⊗B^n,
(5)
H^S=∑nϵnn^n+Eca^†a^+∑n(vnσ^n†a^+vn∗a^†σ^n),
(6)
H^B=∑nα(P^nα22mnα+mnαωnα2R^nα22),B^n=∑αcnαR^nα.
(7)

There is no direct exciton hopping in the article's basic ensemble Hamiltonian. Sparse hopping can be added, but a dense arbitrary exciton coupling matrix would change the computational scaling. The rotating-wave light–matter interaction conserves the total excitation number. Counter-rotating terms and a full gauge-consistent ultrastrong-coupling Hamiltonian are not included in this model.

The energy convention deserves attention. Completing a square for one bath oscillator gives

mω2R^22+cR^=mω22(R^+cmω2)2−c22mω2.
(8)

Consequently the excited-state minimum is lowered by λn=∑αcnα2/(2mnαωnα2) relative to the vertical energy used in the matrix. One can either specify vertical energies directly or add a reorganization counterterm to minimum-to-minimum energies. Both conventions are valid; using both simultaneously counts the shift twice.

Source: Sec. II A, Eqs. (1)–(10). Complex couplings and the explicit counterterm discussion are tutorial generalizations of the real-coupling presentation.

Section 05Excitation manifolds and their dimensions

Define the excitation-number operator

N^exc=a^†a^+∑nn^n.
(9)

For example, [a^†a^,σ^n†a^]=−σ^n†a^, while [n^n,σ^n†a^]=+σ^n†a^. The two terms cancel, so [N^exc,H^SB]=0. Diagonal molecular bath couplings do not change this conclusion.

Let |G⟩=|g1⋯gN;0⟩, |c⟩=|g1⋯gN;1⟩, and |n⟩=|g1⋯en⋯gN;0⟩. Then

B0=(|G⟩),B1=(|c⟩,|1⟩,…,|N⟩),d1=N+1.
(10)

In the second manifold use

B2=(|cc⟩,|c1⟩,…,|cN⟩,|12⟩,|13⟩,…,|N−1,N⟩).
(11)

Here |cc⟩ has two photons; |cn⟩ has one photon and one excited molecule; |nm⟩ has two distinct excited molecules and no photon. Thus

d2=1+N+(N2),D≤2=1+d1+d2=N2+3N+62.
(12)

Linear absorption from the ground state needs only B0⊕B1. Third-order spectra need B2 as well, because excited-state absorption visits it. A two-level molecule does not imply a two-level ensemble, nor does a single-excitation calculation imply a two-excitation spectrum.

Section 06A complete three-molecule single-excitation matrix

For a fixed classical bath configuration define ϵ~n(R)=ϵn+∑αcnαRnα. In B1=(|c⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩,|3⟩),

[H^1(R)]B1=(Ecv1∗v2∗v3∗v1ϵ~100v20ϵ~20v300ϵ~3).
(13)

The bath operator on molecule 2 is [n^2]B1=diag(0,0,1,0). It is not proportional to the identity, so it produces real relative phase fluctuations even though the corresponding matrix is diagonal.

The star structure has only N+1 diagonal elements and 2N off-diagonal elements. This is the key computational fact. It remains true when every molecular energy differs and every molecular dipole has a different orientation. Symmetry may be lost while sparsity survives.

Section 07Bright and dark basis transformations

For identical molecular energies but arbitrary fixed couplings, define

V=(∑n|vn|2)1/2,|Bv⟩=1V∑nvn|n⟩.
(14)

Then H^S|c⟩=Ec|c⟩+V|Bv⟩. Any molecular state orthogonal to |Bv⟩ is dark with respect to this cavity mode. For equal real couplings and three molecules, an explicit orthonormal basis is

|B⟩=|1⟩+|2⟩+|3⟩3,|D1⟩=|1⟩−|2⟩2,|D2⟩=|1⟩+|2⟩−2|3⟩6.
(15)

Using columns that contain these new basis vectors in the old basis gives

[U^]B1←BBD=(100001/31/21/601/3−1/21/601/30−2/6).
(16)

One checks U^†U^=I^, then transforms by [H^]BD=U^†[H^]B1U^. For the symmetric bare Hamiltonian,

[H^]BD=(Ec3v003vϵ0000ϵ0000ϵ).
(17)

A bath configuration generally makes ϵ~n unequal. The bare bright–dark basis still exists, but no longer diagonalizes the instantaneous molecular block. Bath-induced bright–dark couplings must not be discarded merely because the bare cavity coupling has rank one.

Section 08Polariton eigenvalues and a useful derivative identity

The nontrivial block in (|c⟩,|Bv⟩) is

[H^](c,Bv)=(EcVVϵ),E±=Ec+ϵ2±δ2+4V22,δ=Ec−ϵ.
(18)

This follows by solving (Ec−E)(ϵ−E)−V2=0. The full splitting is ΔE=δ2+4V2; only at resonance is it 2V. For equal couplings V=N|v|.

The molecular fractions are obtained without memorizing an angle convention:

X+2=∂E+∂ϵ=12(1−δΔE),X−2=12(1+δΔE).
(19)

The equality between the derivative and the molecular population is the Hellmann–Feynman identity. The photonic fractions are C±2=1−X±2. At resonance both are one half, irrespective of eigenvector phase conventions.

Section 09What diagonal polaron decoupling does—and does not—remove

For independent, identical local bath fluctuations, a normalized polariton with uniform matter component satisfies

⟨±|H^SBint|±⟩=X±2N∑nB^n.
(20)

Its diagonal fluctuation variance is X±4⟨B^n2⟩/N, because cross correlations between different local baths vanish. The corresponding diagonal reorganization scale is

λ±diag=X±4Nλ,λ±diag=λ4Nat resonance.
(21)

This is a statement about a particular projected diagonal coupling. The transformed bath operators also have off-diagonal elements. For one dark state |D⟩=∑ndn|n⟩,

⟨D|H^SBint|±⟩=X±N∑ndn∗B^n.
(22)

An individual channel becomes small with increasing ensemble size, but the number of dark channels grows. Therefore diagonal narrowing does not prove that all relaxation disappears. This distinction becomes especially important when interpreting coherence lifetimes in the later PNAS paper.

Section 10Deriving the matrix-free single-excitation action

Write |c⟩B1=(cc,c1,…,cN)T and |y⟩=H^1|c⟩. Direct multiplication of the star matrix gives

yc=Eccc+∑nvn∗cn,yn=ϵ~ncn+vncc.
(23)

The algorithm is one dot product, one diagonal multiplication, and one vector addition. It requires O(N) arithmetic and O(N) storage. It is exactly the dense product; no approximation has entered.

For a concrete check, take N=2, Ec=0, ϵ~=(1,2), v=(3,4), and |c⟩=(1,i,2)T. The result is

|y⟩=(8+3i3+i8).
(24)

This small test catches a wrong conjugation in the cavity row. For complex couplings, the upper row contains vn∗, while the lower cavity column contains vn.

# Ordered coordinates: [photon, molecule 1, ..., molecule N].
y = np.empty_like(c)
y[0] = Ec*c[0] + np.vdot(v, c[1:])
y[1:] = eps*c[1:] + v*c[0]

Source: Sec. III A, Eqs. (22)–(30). The small numerical example and complex-coupling check are independently derived here.

Section 11Deriving the complete two-excitation action

Let the coefficient groups be ccc, ccn, and cnm with n<m. Apply each term of the Hamiltonian to these basis states. An exciton can turn into a photon, or a photon can excite an unoccupied molecule. Two identical molecular excitations on one site are forbidden.

ycc=2Ecccc+2∑nvn∗ccn,ycn=(Ec+ϵ~n)ccn+2vnccc+∑m≠nvm∗c{n,m},ynm=(ϵ~n+ϵ~m)cnm+vmccn+vnccm,n<m.
(25)

The braces in c{n,m} mean “store the unordered pair in ascending order.” For example, the amplitude entering |c1⟩ from |12⟩ is v2∗c12: molecule 2 emits the photon, while molecule 1 remains excited. Interchanging these couplings is an easy indexing error.

There are N connections from |cc⟩ to |cn⟩, and two connections for every molecular pair. A loop over pairs can update both endpoint coefficients in one pass. Its cost is O(N2)=O(d2), not O(N4)=O(d22).

For two molecules, the full block in (|cc⟩,|c1⟩,|c2⟩,|12⟩) is

(2Ec2v1∗2v2∗02v1Ec+ϵ~10v2∗2v20Ec+ϵ~2v1∗0v2v1ϵ~1+ϵ~2).
(26)

A matrix-free program should be checked against this matrix before being run for thousands of molecules.

Section 12The dipole operation is sparse too

For a chosen probe polarization, let dn be the projected transition dipole. Write

μ^+=∑ndnσ^n†,μ^−=(μ^+)†,μ^=μ^++μ^−.
(27)

The dipole changes the molecular excitation number but does not change photon number. Thus

μ^+|G⟩=∑ndn|n⟩,μ^+|c⟩=∑ndn|cn⟩,μ^+|n⟩=∑m≠ndm|nm⟩.
(28)

Projected into the space through two excitations, the only nonzero output groups of μ^+|c⟩ are

yn=dncG,ycn=dncc,ynm=dmcn+dncm.
(29)

The adjoint formulas give μ^−. In particular, a dipole does not turn |cc⟩ into |cn⟩: that operation changes photon number and is performed by the light–matter Hamiltonian, not the molecular dipole. This distinction is important for keeping optical pathway amplitudes correct.

The optical polarization dn and cavity coupling vn need not have identical orientation factors. They coincide only when the probe and cavity field polarizations, spatial phases, and dipole conventions justify it.

Section 13Storage and arithmetic are different costs

For a single-excitation ket, a dense matrix has (N+1)2 entries while the state has only N+1. The matrix-free action needs only the diagonal and the coupling vector. For a double-excitation ket, both the state and the sparse action scale as N2. This is a major reduction, but it does not remove the N2 state-space growth itself.

Object or operation Single excitation Through two excitations
One state vector O(N) O(N2)
Dense Hamiltonian storage O(N2) O(N4)
Matrix-free Hamiltonian action O(N) O(N2)
One dense density operator O(N2) O(N4)
One forward–backward pair O(N) O(N2)

A complex128 value uses 16 bytes. Multiply the state-vector memory by every simultaneously retained forward/backward vector, Chebyshev workspace, trajectory, and time branch before estimating a production run. Bath coordinate and momentum arrays can dominate even when the quantum state is compact.

The “linear in the number of states” result refers to the operator action. It does not mean linear in molecule count in every excitation sector, nor does it include the cost of converging an ensemble average.

Section 14Why a polynomial can replace a matrix exponential

For a fixed bath configuration during a substep,

|c(t+Δt)⟩=e−iH^QΔt/ℏ|c(t)⟩.
(30)

One could diagonalize H^Q, but rebuilding its eigenvectors at every nuclear time step defeats the purpose of a sparse representation. Instead approximate the scalar function f(E)=e−iEΔt/ℏ by a polynomial on an interval containing the spectrum. Applying that polynomial to H^Q requires only repeated Hamiltonian actions.

For Hermitian H^Q, the spectral theorem makes the error transparent. If |f(E)−p(E)|≤ε for every eigenvalue, then

‖(f(H^Q)−p(H^Q))|c⟩‖≤ε∥|c⟩∥.
(31)

Chebyshev polynomials are useful because they remain bounded on [−1,1], admit a stable three-term recurrence, and have known expansion coefficients for the exponential. They are not an excuse to ignore time dependence in the Hamiltonian.

Section 15Rescale the spectrum before applying the recurrence

Choose lower and upper energy bounds Emin and Emax, with a small safety margin. Define

b=Emax+Emin2,a=Emax−Emin2>0,X^=H^Q−bI^a,z=aΔtℏ.
(32)

Every eigenvalue of X^ should lie in [−1,1]. Then

e−iH^QΔt/ℏ=e−ibΔt/ℏe−izX^.
(33)

The scalar b gives an exactly evaluated phase. The parameter z measures the spectral half-width times the step, not the absolute optical energy times the step.

If the interval has zero width, the Hamiltonian is proportional to the identity and the answer is just a scalar phase; there is no reason to divide by zero in the rescaling. Conversely, using bounds that are too narrow can make the Chebyshev recurrence grow rapidly outside its stable interval.

Section 16Deriving the Chebyshev coefficients

Chebyshev polynomials satisfy Tm(cos⁡θ)=cos⁡(mθ). Their weighted orthogonality on [−1,1] becomes ordinary cosine orthogonality after x=cos⁡θ. The Jacobi–Anger expansion therefore gives

e−izx=J0(z)+2∑m=1∞(−i)mJm(z)Tm(x),−1≤x≤1,
(34)

where Jm is the Bessel function of the first kind. One way to see the coefficient is to multiply by cos⁡(mθ), integrate from zero to π, and use

1π∫0πe−izcos⁡θcos⁡(mθ)dθ=(−i)mJm(z).
(35)

The zero-order term carries no factor of two because the constant cosine has a different normalization. Hence the propagator is

U^(Δt)=e−ibΔt/ℏ[J0(z)I^+2∑m=1∞(−i)mJm(z)Tm(X^)].
(36)

There is no diagonalization in this formula. Only the scalar Bessel coefficients and the action of X^ on vectors are needed.

Source: Sec. III B, Eqs. (31)–(36). The integral derivation and explicit norm bound are supplied here as supporting mathematics.

Section 17The actual vector recurrence

Set |q0⟩=|c⟩, |q1⟩=X^|c⟩. From Tm+1(x)=2xTm(x)−Tm−1(x),

|qm+1⟩=2X^|qm⟩−|qm−1⟩.
(37)

Accumulate

|c′⟩=e−ibΔt/ℏ[J0(z)|q0⟩+2∑m=1M(−i)mJm(z)|qm⟩].
(38)

At each order the calculation needs the previous two recurrence vectors and the accumulating result, not all M vectors. Memory therefore remains proportional to state size. A useful implementation computes X^|q⟩=(H^Q|q⟩−b|q⟩)/a by calling the matrix-free Hamiltonian routine.

Check a simple eigenket |E⟩. The recurrence becomes Tm((E−b)/a)|E⟩, and the accumulated result should be e−iEΔt/ℏ|E⟩. This test detects incorrect signs in (−i)m immediately.

Section 18Convergence, safe energy bounds, and the “four terms” observation

If the spectrum is contained in the chosen interval, ∥Tm(X^)∥≤1. Therefore

∥U^−U^M∥≤2∑m=M+1∞|Jm(z)|.
(39)

The required order grows with |z|. The paper reports that a small number of terms was sufficient for its small-z substeps; this is not a universal four-term rule. In production, increase the order or decrease the step and compare observables, not just the norm of one vector.

A general safe interval follows from Gershgorin bounds:

ℓ=mini(Hii−∑j≠i|Hij|),u=maxi(Hii+∑j≠i|Hij|),ℓ≤Eα≤u.
(40)

Choose the numerical lower bound no larger than ℓ and the upper bound no smaller than u. For a star Hamiltonian they are inexpensive but can be conservative. A sharper enclosure uses the diagonal range and the norm of the off-diagonal star, which is V:

min(Ec,ϵ~1,…)−V≤E≤max(Ec,ϵ~1,…)+V.
(41)

For Gaussian disorder the support is unbounded; a fixed bound based only on a few standard deviations is not mathematically guaranteed. Inspect each sampled configuration or provide an adaptive safety check. A converged polynomial of the wrong frozen Hamiltonian is still the wrong time evolution.

Section 19Separate manifolds without losing relative optical phases

Write the system Hamiltonian as a direct sum and choose a reference energy Eref per excitation:

H^Q=⨁q=02(qErefI^q+ΔH^q).
(42)

Within each block,

U^q(Δt)=e−iqErefΔt/ℏe−iΔH^qΔt/ℏ.
(43)

The second exponential can use a much narrower Chebyshev interval. The first factor must either be retained or tracked analytically. It is not globally irrelevant when a density operator contains coherence between different manifolds.

For a block ρ^qr=Π^qρ^Π^r, the reference phase is

ρ^qr(t)=e−i(q−r)Ereft/ℏρ^~qr(t).
(44)

A population block has q=r, so the phase cancels. An optical coherence has q−r=±1, so omitting the phase shifts the spectrum. The alternative is a rotating-frame calculation with the optical frequency axes restored afterward. Both procedures are valid if carried through consistently.

Source: Sec. III C, Eqs. (37)–(44), and Appendix C.

Section 20Time-dependent baths: polynomial accuracy is only one error

The exact propagator for moving nuclei is time ordered:

U^(t+Δt,t)=T^exp⁡[−iℏ∫tt+ΔtH^Q(R(s))ds].
(45)

Using exp⁡[−iH^Q(R(t))Δt/ℏ] freezes the bath at the start. A midpoint approximation uses R(t+Δt/2) and, for a sufficiently smooth Hamiltonian, has higher local accuracy. Neither becomes exact merely by increasing Chebyshev order.

There are at least four independently controllable numerical errors: nuclear integration, time ordering of the quantum Hamiltonian, polynomial truncation, and splitting between radiative and Hamiltonian evolution. Keep a reference calculation where each is reduced separately. When a result changes with a smaller nuclear step but not with a higher polynomial order, the polynomial is not the limiting error.

A large carrier energy can be removed analytically. Rapid bath fluctuations, rapid nonadiabatic changes, and a rapidly varying external pulse cannot be removed by that same energy shift.

Section 21How PLDM produces forward–backward trajectories

The exact density operator contains a forward propagator and a backward propagator:

ρ^S(t)=TrB[e−iH^SBt/ℏρ^SB(0)e+iH^SBt/ℏ].
(46)

In a path-integral representation, introduce forward and backward nuclear paths |RF⟩, |RB⟩, their mean |R⟩=(|RF⟩+|RB⟩)/2, and difference |ΔR⟩=|RF⟩−|RB⟩. Expanding the action to first order in the difference variables causes their integrations to impose classical-like equations for the mean nuclear path. The mapping variables on the two branches remain distinct. This is the partial linearization underlying PLDM.

For a scalar potential term,

V(R+ΔR/2)−V(R−ΔR/2)=ΔRV′(R)+O(ΔR3).
(47)

Keeping the first term is the approximation; it is not a weak-coupling expansion of the light–matter Hamiltonian. The complete mapping path integral additionally contains electronic coherent-state overlaps and endpoint factors. Those factors explain why a single trajectory cannot simply be interpreted as one normalized molecular wavefunction.

The useful computational representation is

ρ^est=w|f⟩⟨b|,ρ^S≈⟨ρ^est⟩trajectories.
(48)

Here w includes initial-state and mapping weights. Forward and backward vectors are independent sampling objects but interact through the shared nuclear force.

Section 22Mapping coordinates, coefficients, and forces

For a real symmetric electronic matrix, define dimensionless mapping variables by ca=(xa+ipa)/2. The quadratic mapping Hamiltonian is

Hmap=12∑abHab(R)(xaxb+papb).
(49)

Hamilton's equations give x˙a=ℏ−1∑bHabpb and p˙a=−ℏ−1∑bHabxb, hence

iℏddt|f⟩=H^Q(R)|f⟩,−iℏddt⟨b|=⟨b|H^Q(R).
(50)

The bra equation has the opposite sign because it is a backward amplitude. If the program stores the conjugate ket instead, its equation has the same Schrödinger sign as the forward ket. Mixing these storage conventions produces incorrect phases.

For the local HTC bath, the PLDM force in the coefficient convention of the article is

R˙nα=Pnα/mnα,P˙nα=−mnαωnα2Rnα−cnα⟨f|n^n|f⟩+⟨b|n^n|b⟩2.
(51)

In the two-excitation sector, n^n counts every configuration containing molecule n, not just |n⟩. Factors associated with mapping-coordinate normalization must be kept consistent with the endpoint estimator. These formulas must not be combined with another method's zero-point correction without rederiving the force and estimator together.

Source: Sec. IV A, Eqs. (50)–(64). The mean/difference-path expansion explains the approximation rather than replacing the full PLDM path-integral derivation.

Section 23Thermal Wigner sampling of harmonic modes

For a harmonic mode, the normalized Wigner density in phase-space coordinates (R,P) is

Wβ(R,P)=tanh⁡(βℏω/2)πℏexp⁡[−tanh⁡(βℏω/2)ℏ(mωR2+P2mω)].
(52)

It integrates to one under dRdP. Reading off the two Gaussian widths gives

⟨R2⟩=ℏ2mωcoth⁡βℏω2,⟨P2⟩=mℏω2coth⁡βℏω2,⟨RP⟩W=0.
(53)

At high temperature these reduce to kBT/(mω2) and mkBT. At zero temperature they retain zero-point widths. Draw independent normal variates and multiply by the square roots of these variances. Treating wavenumbers as angular frequencies without the 2πc conversion changes the sampled dynamics and memory time.

Wigner sampling reproduces the thermal harmonic initial distribution. It does not make the subsequent classical propagation exact for an arbitrary coupled quantum system.

Section 24Spectral density and discretization checks

Adopt the coordinate-coupling convention

J(ω)=π2∑αcα2mαωαδ(ω−ωα),λ=1π∫0∞J(ω)ωdω.
(54)

For the Debye/Drude form used in the paper,

J(ω)=2λγωω2+γ2.
(55)

A quadrature with frequencies ωα and weights wα can be implemented by

cα=2mαωαπJ(ωα)wα.
(56)

Then check ∑αcα2/(2mαωα2) against the intended λ. A finite upper cutoff omits part of the integral, so either accept that explicitly as a changed bath or adjust the discretization consistently. Verify the bath correlation function over the complete time range of the spectrum; checking only the reorganization energy is insufficient.

For example, γ/(2πc)=18cm−1 corresponds to a memory time 1/γ≈295fs, not 1/(18c). This provides a useful unit test.

Section 25Cavity loss and the meaning of an exact substep

With photon number decay rate κ, a common radiative model is

dρ^dt=−iℏ[H^,ρ^]+κ(a^ρ^a^†−12{a^†a^,ρ^}).
(57)

If a linewidth Γc is specified as an energy, κ=Γc/ℏ. A one-photon population decays as e−κt, while its coherence with the vacuum decays as e−κt/2.

The article's Appendix A implements radiative loss through stochastic updates of forward and backward amplitudes. The average of the appropriate updates reproduces the specified loss map. An individual estimator can be complex and need not preserve its trace. A symmetric composition is

eΔt(L^H+L^c)=eΔtL^c/2eΔtL^HeΔtL^c/2+O(Δt3).
(58)

An exact radiative substep does not remove the splitting error or the PLDM approximation. Also distinguish one collective jump a^ from a sum of independent transition-resolved jump channels. Their populations can agree while their coherence-transfer terms differ. The 2023 notes derive this distinction explicitly.

Section 26Deriving the linear response from a weak probe

Let the external field enter as H^probe(t)=−E(t)μ^. In the interaction picture,

dρ^Idt=iℏE(t)[μ^I(t),ρ^I(t)].
(59)

Insert the equilibrium density on the right-hand side to obtain the first-order perturbation,

δρ^I(t)=iℏ∫−∞tE(s)[μ^I(s),ρ^eq]ds.
(60)

Taking the expectation value of the dipole gives the causal response kernel

R(1)(t)=iℏΘ(t)TrSB{μ^I(t)[μ^,ρ^eq]}.
(61)

The sign depends on the chosen probe Hamiltonian and transform convention. Throughout this tutorial the probe interaction is −Eμ^. Comparison with a plotted spectrum requires matching the article's global response phase as well as its frequency-axis convention.

For a factorized electronic ground state and thermal bath, ρ^eq=|G⟩⟨G|⊗ρ^B. The two commutator terms are |μG⟩⟨G| and its adjoint, where

|μG⟩=μ^+|G⟩=∑ndn|n⟩.
(62)

The probe therefore prepares an optical coherence, not a normalized excited-state population.

Section 27From one propagated optical ket to a spectrum

For a fixed bath-free Hamiltonian with the ground energy set to zero, define

C(t)=⟨μG|e−iH^1t/ℏ|μG⟩=∑α|⟨α|μG⟩|2e−iEαt/ℏ.
(63)

The positive-frequency absorption shape can be obtained from the real part of the one-sided transform of C(t), up to overall physical prefactors. With phenomenological energy half-width η>0,

A(E)=−Im⟨μG|(E+iη−H^1)−1|μG⟩=∑αη|⟨α|μG⟩|2(E−Eα)2+η2.
(64)

The resolvent follows by integrating ei(E+iη)t/ℏe−iH^1t/ℏ. Its Lorentzian weights provide an exact small-system reference for the time-domain transform, not a substitute for a dynamical molecular bath.

For equal molecular dipoles aligned with the cavity, |μG⟩=dN|B⟩. At resonance the two bright peaks each carry Nd2/2, and the total oscillator strength remains Nd2. A program that normalizes each spectrum independently cannot test this sum rule.

Source: Sec. III D and Sec. IV B. The resolvent calculation is the bath-free teaching reference.

Section 28Finite time windows, resolution, and energy restoration

The recorded response is finite. If it is multiplied by the paper's cosine window w(t)=cos⁡(πt/2T), the transform is

C~(E)=∫0Tdtw(t)eiEt/ℏC(t).
(65)

Windowing reduces sharp truncation artifacts but changes the lineshape. The frequency sampling scale is approximately ΔE=2πℏ/T. Zero-padding makes a smoother plotted grid; it does not add late-time information or improve the physical resolution.

With a time step Δt, the Nyquist angular-frequency bound is π/Δt. A rotating-frame response must be interpreted relative to its carrier. If C(t)=e−iEreft/ℏC~(t), then its spectrum is shifted by +Eref. Retaining a shifted Hamiltonian and labeling the resulting axis as an unshifted absolute energy is incorrect.

Check the sign convention using an artificial C(t)=e−iE0t/ℏ. Its peak should occur at positive E0 with the transform written above. This single-frequency test is more reliable than memorizing FFT sign conventions.

Section 29Static energy disorder is not dynamical dephasing

A static ensemble can have ϵn=ϵ¯+δϵn, with independent Gaussian fluctuations of standard deviation σ. These offsets are sampled once per realization and remain fixed during a trajectory. A local harmonic bath produces time-dependent fluctuations and memory. They are distinct sources of broadening.

In a symmetric bright state, the mean first-order static energy shift is N−1∑nδϵn, whose variance is σ2/N. Nevertheless, disorder also mixes bright and dark states. This variance argument is valid perturbatively; it is not an exact spectral linewidth formula for arbitrary disorder.

The physically meaningful ensemble average is performed on response functions or spectra with consistent normalization:

A(E)―=∫dϵP(ϵ)A(E;ϵ),
(66)

where dϵ denotes integration over the components of the energy-disorder coordinate ket. In general, diagonalizing the averaged Hamiltonian does not give the averaged spectrum. The resolvent and exponential are nonlinear functions of the disorder realization.

Section 30Orientation disorder: define the angular measure first

For cavity polarization |ec⟩, write vn=v0cos⁡θn for real projected dipoles. The exact collective coupling of a particular realization is

V2=∑n|vn|2=v02∑ncos2⁡θn.
(67)

Opposite signs do not cancel this norm. They change the phases of the bright molecular combination. For isotropic three-dimensional orientations the polar-angle measure is p(θ)dθ=12sin⁡θdθ, so

⟨cos⁡θ⟩=0,⟨cos2⁡θ⟩=13.
(68)

A uniform angle in a plane instead gives 1/2. A distribution uniform in θ is not isotropic on a sphere. When reproducing a figure, use the distribution stated for that calculation; do not silently substitute a different dimensional angular measure.

An efficient isotropic sampler draws u uniformly from [−1,1] and uses cos⁡θ=u. For linearly polarized absorption the probe factor dn must also reflect its own polarization. A molecular state can be dark to the cavity but bright to a differently polarized probe.

Section 31Compare fixed single-molecule coupling with fixed collective splitting

At fixed v0, increasing N increases the collective splitting as N. At fixed V, the individual coupling must decrease as 1/N. These are different physical sequences and must not be mixed in a scaling plot.

For uniform couplings,

v0(N)=ΔEres2N.
(69)

With orientations, fixing the actual splitting of each sampled realization instead requires v0=V/∑ncos2⁡θn. Using V3/N fixes the isotropic expectation approximately, not the exact realization-by-realization coupling.

Finite-size convergence means an observable stops changing along a specified physical sequence. Computational cost scaling means the number of operations grows in a specified way. Neither statement implies the other. The matrix-free method makes large N accessible; convergence still has to be demonstrated for the spectrum and bath parameters of interest.

Section 32Reading the paper's numerical results

The article uses the HTC model to compare collective linear spectra as molecule number, energetic disorder, angular disorder, and photon loss change. Its central numerical evidence is that the reorganized propagation reproduces reference behavior while avoiding the dense matrix bottleneck. Read the line shapes together with the stated scaling protocol: a larger splitting caused by increasing V is not identical to narrowing at fixed V.

Location in the paper What to inspect What it does not establish by itself
Fig. 1 and Fig. 3 Sparse Hamiltonian and dipole patterns A reduction in Hilbert-space dimension
Fig. 2; Appendix B Chebyshev coefficient behavior and propagation checks A universal time step or polynomial order
Sec. V, Figs. 4–8 Collective spectra with the specified bath and disorder models Exact dynamics for every molecular environment
Appendix C, Fig. 9 Carrier-frequency shifting and restored line shapes Permission to drop intermanifold phases

The model uses a slowly relaxing Debye bath and room-temperature sampling for its main examples. Numerical settings belong to the individual figure and convergence test. They should be copied from the article's computational section, not inferred from a different paper in the series.

Source: Secs. IV C–V, numerical spectra, and Appendices B–C. The interpretation in the third column separates algorithmic claims from physical approximations.

Section 33Interactive scale and dimension check

This panel evaluates algebraic dimensions, collective mixing, and storage for one complex128 vector. It does not propagate a bath or estimate total runtime. Energies in the coupling fields are in meV. The determinant of the two-by-two bright block gives the splitting; no fitted linewidth is used.

With the default inputs, the resonant splitting is 100 meV and the beat period is about 41.36 fs. The polynomial parameter is about 0.0912. A small value suggests rapid convergence of the exponential expansion, but the number of terms must still be checked.

Section 34A validation ladder before a production calculation

Start with identities that cannot be hidden by ensemble averaging. Build the Hamiltonian from tensor-product operators, project it into the chosen ordered basis, and compare its action with the sparse routine on several random complex kets. Do the same for the dipole and photon-loss operators. Include a double-excitation test; a single-excitation test cannot detect a missing 2.

Next compare one Chebyshev step against an eigendecomposition of a small Hermitian matrix. Test an energy shift of several orders of magnitude, retaining the analytic phase. Repeat with both real and complex couplings and with nondegenerate site energies.

Then check physics in progressively harder limits: bath-free oscillator strengths, photon-only decay, zero light–matter coupling, independent thermal bath variances, and short trajectory ensembles. Finally vary the bath discretization, quantum step, nuclear step, polynomial order, trajectory count, and time window separately. A small trace error is useful, but is not a convergence certificate for a spectrum.

The downloadable code follows the first two levels. It is deliberately small enough to inspect. Its tests compare two independently constructed representations, not two calls to the same sparse routine.

Section 35Teaching Python and its scope

Download collective_linear_teaching.py

python collective_linear_teaching.py --test
python collective_linear_teaching.py --demo --output linear_demo.csv

The test command checks Hermiticity, single- and double-manifold matrix-free actions, dipole actions, Chebyshev propagation, and oscillator-strength conservation. The demo diagonalizes a modest disordered single-excitation Hamiltonian and saves a broadened absorption spectrum. It requires NumPy and SciPy.

There are no molecular trajectories, PLDM mapping weights, or fitted bath kernels in that demo. The broadening is explicitly a chosen Lorentzian half-width. Changing that number cannot stand in for changing λ, γ, or the bath temperature in the article's dynamical calculations.

Section 36Worked exercises

1. Why is the two-excitation dimension not simply (N+1)²?

A photon can occupy the same mode twice, but a molecule cannot be excited twice. There is one two-photon state, N one-photon/one-molecule states, and N(N−1)/2 unordered molecular pairs. Therefore d₂=1+N+N(N−1)/2. For N=3 this is seven. Counting ordered pairs would count each two-molecule state twice and would incorrectly include three forbidden same-site double excitations.

2. Check the two-molecule sparse multiplication numerically.

Use the matrix in the single-manifold section with Ec=0, site energies 1 and 2, couplings 3 and 4, and coefficients (1,i,2). The photon component is 3i+8. Molecule 1 gives 3+i. Molecule 2 gives 4+4=8. Changing the second coupling to 4i puts −4i in the photon row and +4i in the molecular cavity column. This is a simple Hermiticity test for complex couplings.

3. Derive the cavity-dark criterion for unequal dipoles.

For a molecular ket with coefficients dₙ, the cavity amplitude generated by the Hamiltonian is the inner product of the coupling ket with that molecular ket. It vanishes when the two are orthogonal. Thus darkness is orthogonality to the coupling-weighted bright vector, not necessarily a zero unweighted sum of coefficients. When all couplings are equal and real, the condition reduces to a zero sum.

4. Find the splitting for N=25 and v=10 meV at resonance.

The collective coupling is √25 × 10=50 meV. The full splitting is twice that value, 100 meV. Dividing 2πℏ by 100 meV gives a beat period of about 41.36 fs. The quantity ℏ divided by the splitting is about 6.58 fs and is not the full period; it is the inverse angular-frequency scale.

5. Derive the diagonal reorganization reduction at resonance.

Each local bath enters a polariton diagonal element with coefficient 1/(2N). Reorganization energy is quadratic in coupling, so N independent baths contribute N × λ/(4N²)=λ/(4N). This calculation does not sum transition rates into N−1 dark states and therefore cannot conclude that all relaxation vanishes.

6. What happens if a Chebyshev eigenvalue lies outside [−1,1]?

For x>1, the polynomial can be written as cosh[m arcosh(x)], which grows exponentially with m. The bounded-polynomial error estimate no longer applies. Increasing the expansion order can make a bad enclosure worse rather than better. Expand the energy interval first, then converge the order.

7. Is a carrier-energy shift physically irrelevant?

A single common identity shift cancels from density evolution. The useful manifold shift is proportional to excitation number, however, and optical coherences connect different excitation numbers. Their relative phase contains the carrier. Retain that phase or restore the frequency origin after transforming a rotating-frame response. Population-only tests cannot catch an omitted optical carrier.

8. Show why zero-padding does not improve physical resolution.

Appending zeros changes the spacing at which the finite-time transform is evaluated. It does not change the integral's upper limit T or add information about late-time decay. The linewidth limitation from the time window therefore remains. Compare spectra at a longer propagation time to establish resolution convergence; compare zero-padding only to check interpolation and plotting.

9. What is the orientation factor for a random three-dimensional ensemble?

Use u=cosθ, uniformly distributed on [−1,1]. Its second moment is one half of the integral of u² over that interval, giving 1/3. The first moment is zero. Therefore the expected squared collective coupling is Nv₀²/3, not zero. Averaging signed amplitudes before constructing the bright state confuses a zero first moment with a nonzero norm.

10. Why is one optical coherence enough in the bath-free reference?

The initial positive-frequency coherence is the rank-one operator formed from the dipole-prepared ket and the ground bra. The ground bra is stationary after its energy is set to zero. Propagating the ket and contracting with the dipole therefore evaluates the correlation exactly. This simplification is not a license to discard the backward bath history in a general PLDM trajectory.

11. Estimate the state storage for N=1000 through two excitations.

D=(1000²+3×1000+6)/2=501503. One complex128 vector occupies 8024048 bytes, about 8.024 MB in decimal units. A forward–backward pair is about 16.05 MB before adding polynomial workspace, bath arrays, or time branches. The dense density matrix would require over four terabytes. Matrix-free propagation avoids storing that density matrix, not the half-million-amplitude ket.

12. Design a test that distinguishes polynomial error from frozen-bath error.

First hold a bath configuration fixed and increase the Chebyshev order until comparison with the exact matrix exponential stops changing. Then propagate a prescribed smooth time-dependent bath path with successively smaller time steps, keeping the polynomial tightly converged at every step. The remaining step dependence measures time-ordering error. Adding self-consistent nuclear motion introduces a third error that should be tested separately.

Section 37How this paper connects to the other projects

The 2025 nonlinear-spectra paper uses the same sparse Hamiltonian and dipole actions but must handle repeated optical interactions and a two-excitation space. Its factorized importance sampling is a different reduction from the one derived here.

The transport paper introduces multiple cavity modes and position-dependent phases. A star-matrix multiply is then replaced by Fourier transforms on a uniform molecular grid. The 2023 paper provides the trajectory-loss and nonlinear-response foundations. The symmetry-adapted HEOM project instead compresses an explicitly quantum hierarchy when permutation symmetry permits it; it does not rely on the same mixed quantum–classical approximation.

The practical lesson is to separate three layers: the physical model, the dynamical approximation, and the linear-algebra implementation. An efficient implementation can preserve a chosen approximation exactly without making that approximation exact for the original molecule–cavity–bath problem.
